# Blood groups and transfusion (`blood_groups_transfusion`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by blood_circulation, heat_sterilisation, microscope, refrigeration
- Core idea: Donor red cells carry antigens that a recipient’s antibodies may attack, causing potentially fatal haemolysis. ABO and RhD typing, an antibody screen and compatibility testing guide selection. Visible clumping reveals some mismatches, but a negative bedside slide test does not establish compatibility. Group O red cells lack A and B antigens; group O whole blood also contains donor plasma whose antibodies may attack the recipient’s cells. Citrate prevents clotting, while sterile collection, donor screening and controlled cold storage address separate hazards. Sterile intravenous crystalloid can restore volume but cannot carry oxygen.
- Pitfalls:
  - Animal blood (the lamb's blood transfusions of 1667 ended in deaths and a ban)
  - Assuming relatives always match
  - Skipping the test in an emergency
  - Passing on syphilis, malaria or jaundice from the donor
  - Air in the tubing, or running blood in too fast
- History: europe: 1665 – Lower transfuses dog to dog; 1667 Denis gives lamb's blood to a man; banned c. 1670; 1818–1829 Blundell's human-to-human transfusions for bleeding after childbirth; 1832 Latta's saline infusion in cholera; 1901 Landsteiner's blood groups (Vienna); 1902 fourth group (Decastello, Sturli); 1914 citrate (Hustin, Brussels); 1917 Robertson establishes stored-blood depots on the Western Front; americas: 1907 – Ottenberg cross-matches before transfusing; 1914–1915 citrate method (Agote in Buenos Aires, Lewisohn in New York); 1937 Fantus's blood bank in Chicago; 1940 Rhesus factor (Landsteiner, Wiener)
- Read:
  - Karl Landsteiner, Ueber Agglutinationserscheinungen normalen menschlichen Blutes, Wiener klinische Wochenschrift (1901)
  - Douglas Starr, Blood: An Epic History of Medicine and Commerce (1998)
  - Holly Tucker, Blood Work: A Tale of Medicine and Murder in the Scientific Revolution (2011)
